backend.label: Back-end service
backend.blurb: An API with no interface. What will move: data sources, integrations. Rarely the screens, there are none.
backend.example: add a route that reads a book

frontend.label: Web interface
frontend.blurb: An application in a browser. What will move: screens and journeys. Almost never the source of the data.
frontend.example: add a screen that shows a book

mobile.label: Mobile application
mobile.blurb: A native application. What will move: screens and local state, under intermittent connectivity.
mobile.example: add a screen that shows a book

fullstack.label: Front and back in one repository
fullstack.blurb: Two products, one repository. The real question is not their internal structure but what passes between them.
fullstack.example: show a book, from the database to the screen

decision_axis.question: Are you really going to replace your database?
decision_axis.why: This is the question that eliminates the most options. Some architectures exist so you can change database without touching the rest. That is paid for on every route you write. If you will never change it, you are paying for insurance you will not claim.

answers.label: No, never
answers.then: Set hexagonal and Clean aside. You do not have the problem they solve.

answers.label: Maybe a third-party service
answers.then: Isolate that one service. Not the rest.

answers.label: Yes, that is the business
answers.then: Hexagonal is genuinely justified. That is rare.

decision_axis.question: Would your business rules survive a complete change of technology?
decision_axis.short: Is there a domain, or just data?
decision_axis.why: Some architectures isolate business rules from everything else. That still requires rules to exist. A service that reads a table and returns it as JSON has no domain: it has a schema. Adding a domain layer to it creates files that copy rows around.

answers.label: We move data and validate it
answers.then: A folder per feature is more than enough.

answers.label: A few rules that matter
answers.then: Isolate those rules. Not the whole model.

answers.label: Dense rules, discussed with the business
answers.then: Clean or Onion start to make sense.

decision_axis.question: How many people or agents will work on it at the same time?
decision_axis.short: Alone, optimise for cohesion. With several, for parallel work.
decision_axis.why: Arranging by technical layer puts everyone in the same folders: every feature crosses every layer. Arranging by feature gives each person their own folder. This is the most concrete of the four criteria.

answers.label: Two to five
answers.then: Arrange by feature. One folder each.

answers.label: Several teams
answers.then: Autonomous modules with contracts between them.

decision_axis.question: In your previous projects, what changed most often?
decision_axis.short: Put what moves least at the centre.
decision_axis.why: An architecture protects whatever it places at the centre. The classic mistake is protecting what never moves and leaving at the edge what changes every week. You only notice after two years.

answers.label: Screens and journeys
answers.then: Arrange by feature, not by layer.

answers.label: The business rules
answers.then: Isolate them, with tests that know no technology.

answers.label: External integrations
answers.then: That is where, and only where, ports are justified.

feature-modules.name: A folder per feature
feature-modules.plain: Everything about books lives in the « books » folder. Everything about loans lives in « loans ». You do not arrange by technical nature.
feature-modules.cost: Almost nothing. One rule only: a folder does not rummage inside another, it goes through what the other publishes.
feature-modules.buys: Two people work without colliding. Removing a feature means removing a folder.
feature-modules.wrong_when: When two features share many rules: they end up copied, or the « shared » folder becomes the dumping ground.
feature-modules.verdict: The reasonable default. Start here. You climb into abstraction when a precise pain demands it, not before.
feature-modules.grows_into: A module whose rules grow dense hardens on its own, without touching the others.
feature-modules.migration_cost: Low and local. You harden one folder at a time, the others do not move. It is the only option you can leave piece by piece.
migration_triggers: The same business rule appears in two modules -> pull it into a shared module, once.
You really must replace one integration -> put a port on that one, not on the rest.
A module passes a dozen rules discussed with the business -> isolate ITS domain, that one alone.

layered.name: Arranged by technical layer
layered.plain: All controllers together, all services together, all data access together. You arrange by nature, not by subject.
layered.cost: Low, and familiar. Three folders, one rule about direction.
layered.buys: Everything has an obvious place. A newcomer knows where to look.
layered.wrong_when: As soon as several people work on it. A single feature touches all three folders, so everyone edits the same places.
layered.verdict: Honest for a one-person project. It is the layout that parallelises worst.
layered.grows_into: Moving to a per-feature split means moving almost every file.
layered.migration_cost: High and global. Every feature is scattered across three folders: you do not migrate piece by piece.
migration_triggers: Two people regularly get in each other's way in the same folders -> the split is already wrong.
You spend a long time looking for where to put a new rule -> the layer says nothing about the subject.

hexagonal.name: Hexagonal (ports and adapters)
hexagonal.plain: The core of the software says « I need someone who knows how to store a book » without knowing whether that is a database, a file or a remote service. You plug one or the other in behind it.
hexagonal.cost: High, and every single time. Six files where three were enough. Half of them only pass information from one floor to the next.
hexagonal.buys: Change database without touching the rules. Test the rules with no database at all. Real, but only on the day you actually change.
hexagonal.wrong_when: When you will change nothing. A database chosen once is not a plug, it is a decision. The interface around it then serves nobody.
hexagonal.verdict: Justified when plugging different systems together IS the business. Over-engineering everywhere else, and everywhere else is the common case.
hexagonal.grows_into: Nothing pushes you out of it: you keep the ceremony, even once it serves nothing.
hexagonal.migration_cost: There is no going back. You live with it. That is why this choice is made late, not early.
tree: `-- adapters/       the real database, the real HTTP
files_for_example: + a fake repository for the tests
migration_triggers: You have not replaced a single adapter in two years -> the cost was paid for nothing, but nobody removes ports.

clean.name: Clean Architecture
clean.plain: Nested circles. Business objects at the centre, use cases around them, then the plugs, then the framework. Everything points inward, never the reverse.
clean.cost: The highest. One file per action, and objects copied at every boundary crossing.
clean.buys: The business rules read without knowing anything about the framework. Changing framework becomes almost free.
clean.wrong_when: When the domain is thin. You get use cases calling one method and objects copying rows: all the ceremony, no benefit.
clean.verdict: For a dense domain, discussed, meant to last years. Rarely the right call for a first version.
clean.grows_into: Like hexagonal: you do not remove layers, you endure them.
clean.migration_cost: The hardest in the catalogue to leave. Reserve it for domains you know are dense BEFORE you start.
migration_triggers: Your use cases only call one method -> the layer carries nothing, but removing it touches everything.

onion.name: Onion
onion.plain: Like Clean, with one layer fewer. The model at the centre, the services around it, the technology on the outside.
onion.cost: Close to Clean, one floor fewer to name.
onion.buys: The same isolation of the domain, with fewer pass-through files.
onion.verdict: If you are hesitating between Clean and Onion, that is not the problem: the problem is that you are not sure you need either.
onion.migration_cost: As hard to leave as Clean.
tree: |-- services/       what you do with them
migration_triggers: Your domain services are empty -> same symptom, same dead end.

feature-sliced.name: Feature-sliced
feature-sliced.plain: Ordered floors: pages at the top, then features, then business objects, then what is shared. A floor only uses the floors below it.
feature-sliced.cost: Low, but it demands discipline: the rule only holds if everyone knows which floor what they write belongs to.
feature-sliced.buys: No more circular imports in a codebase where everything tends to import everything. Removing a feature becomes possible again.
feature-sliced.wrong_when: On an interface of a few screens: there are more floors than features.
feature-sliced.verdict: The most solid for a web interface meant to grow. Excessive below about ten screens.
feature-sliced.grows_into: The floors absorb growth: you add features, not floors.
feature-sliced.migration_cost: Low. The model is built to grow, that is its purpose.
migration_triggers: One floor becomes enormous -> that is an internal split to revisit, not the architecture.

mvvm.name: MVVM
mvvm.plain: The screen has no logic. It watches an object that prepares everything it must display, and that object knows nothing of the screen.
mvvm.cost: Low. It is often what the framework already imposes.
mvvm.buys: Screen logic is testable without launching the interface. It is the most profitable gain on mobile.
mvvm.wrong_when: When the view model becomes the dumping ground where all business logic lands, for want of a layer beneath it.
mvvm.verdict: To be combined with a per-feature split. Never alone on a project that grows.
mvvm.grows_into: Combines with a per-feature split as the number of screens grows.
mvvm.migration_cost: Low. MVVM layers on top, it does not replace.
tree: |-- screens/        what is displayed, no logic
migration_triggers: A view model becomes a dumping ground -> a layer below it is missing, not another pattern.

mvi.name: MVI (unidirectional state)
mvi.plain: The screen has one complete state at any instant. Every gesture produces a new state, never a modification of the old one. The display is only a function of that state.
mvi.cost: Moderate. Many types to declare, and a detour between a gesture and its effect.
mvi.buys: A bug is reproduced by replaying the sequence of gestures. Decisive on mobile, where the system destroys and recreates screens.
mvi.wrong_when: On simple screens: the machinery costs more than the state it protects.
mvi.verdict: For screens with complicated state: long forms, synchronisation, offline mode.
mvi.migration_cost: Low, and reversible screen by screen.
migration_triggers: Simple screens carry the same machinery as complicated ones -> apply it only where the state deserves it.

tokens.title: What you are allowed to draw with
tokens.verbatim: This page does not decide anything and it is not a screen. It shows the values already declared, side by side, so that what a file hides becomes visible: colours nobody can tell apart, a spacing step that repeats the one before it, a pair that cannot carry text. The screens come after, and they may use nothing that is not here.
tokens.colours_head: The colours, and what happens between them
tokens.colours_blurb: Every pair, with its contrast ratio. This is the measurable half of accessibility, and the half a palette can hide until the first screen is built.
tokens.indistinguishable: nearly indistinguishable — two decisions where one was meant
tokens.scale_blurb: Sorted, because an unordered scale hides its own gaps — and its own repetitions.
tokens.no_step: a step away from {name}, which is no step at all
tokens.fonts_blurb: Rendered, not quoted. A font named but never shown tells you nothing about it, and two that read alike are one font too many.

decisions.title: What awaits your decision
decisions.nothing: Nothing awaits arbitration: no blocked issue, none out of reach of the agents, no open spec question.
decisions.waiting: {count} point(s) cannot move without you. The pipeline carries on with the rest.
decisions.verbatim: This page is computed from the store and the file policy, not written. An issue whose scope no role can take appears here even if nobody reported it.
decisions.spec_blurb: Choices submitted by Product. Nothing is decomposed before your answer.
decisions.blocked_blurb: These issues hold their reservations for as long as they stay blocked.
decisions.blocked_why: This issue is stopped in {phase} and waits to be released. As long as it stays there it holds its reservations and blocks any issue that crosses them.
decisions.orphan_blurb: Scope entirely outside the file policy of the writing roles. next-issues presents them as dispatchable all the same.
decisions.orphan_empty: Every open issue has a role able to take it.
decisions.orphan_why: Its whole scope is outside the file policy of every writing role. No implementer can take it: this is operator work, whether it says so or not.
decisions.moves_note: {count} issue(s) in planned have a role able to take them and await no decision.
decisions.moves_caveat: The points above do not block them, unless their reservations intersect.
decisions.approve: Approve the scope of round {round} for decomposition?
decisions.approve_why: Product declares the scope settled and submits no further choice. Approving freezes the document: phase 2 is refused if its content moves by a single character.
decisions.approve_no: Ask for one more round, saying what is missing

dependency.rejected_blurb: A decision taken in silence is exactly what this page exists to prevent. These were considered and set aside.
dependency.verbatim: Installing is yours, not the pipeline's. No agent adds a dependency: it argues for one and stops. This page is that argument, taken verbatim from the request, with every field the agent measured rather than assumed.
dependency.candidates_blurb: License, weight, upkeep and security surface. A library that does the job and is unmaintained does not do the job.
dependency.commits_note: A dependency on a public input surface becomes part of your security perimeter: its advisories become yours, its maintainers become your maintainers, and removing it later costs more than adding it now. Refusing is a valid answer, and the cost of writing it by hand is stated above so that refusing is an informed choice rather than a reflex.

proposal.does_blurb: {count} features. Every numbered rule is a binding commitment, not an intention.
proposal.not_head: What the product does not do
proposal.not_blurb: {count} named exclusions. What is not written here is assumed built — which is why these are explicit.
proposal.awaits_blurb: {count} choices submitted. Nothing is decomposed before your answer.
proposal.decomposition_blurb: {count} issues. No issue content is written before the agreement.
proposal.design_blurb: Constraints carried into the issues and enforceable in review. These are not suggestions.
proposal.pr_blurb: Transparency commitments. The exposed surfaces are named, not softened.
proposal.verbatim: Text taken verbatim from the proposal, with no rewording: an obliging re-read would open a gap between what you read and what the digest freezes.
proposal.commits_freeze: Approving this document freezes its content.
proposal.commits_nodigest: Phase 2 is bound to this document:
proposal.commits_tail: any decomposition derived from another document, or from this one modified afterwards, is refused by validate-handoff with a non-zero exit code. What this document does not say will not be built; what it says wrongly will be built wrongly.

tokens.name: 1. Tokens
tokens.plain: The raw values: colours, spacing, type sizes, radii, durations. A list of names and values, no component.
tokens.why: Everything else refers to them. Putting them last means everything before carries hardcoded values, and a change of brand is made file by file.
tokens.decide: Where they live, and in what form. A file of CSS variables, a TypeScript object, a style engine's configuration: it does not matter, as long as there is ONE.
tokens.trap: Two sources of truth. Tokens in the code and a palette in the mockup tool, drifting apart in silence.

primitives.name: 2. Primitives
primitives.plain: The bricks with no domain: button, field, label, modal. They know no product rule, only the tokens.
primitives.why: This is the layer where duplication starts. An agent that finds none writes one more button, then another.
primitives.decide: Write them yourself, or take an existing library. See below: that choice is weighed, not guessed.
primitives.trap: A primitive taking a domain prop. From then on it is no longer reusable, and the next one gets copied.

components.name: 3. Product components
components.plain: What knows the domain: a book card, a loan form. They assemble primitives.
components.why: They change often, and that is fine. What must not change often is the two layers beneath.
components.decide: Where they live: your architecture answers that, not this page.
components.trap: A product component redefining a colour instead of using a token.

screens.name: 4. Screens and journeys
screens.plain: The final assembly, and the navigation between assemblies.
screens.why: It is what a user sees, so it is what gets discussed first, and yet it is what gets decided last.
screens.decide: Nothing structural here if the three layers above hold.
screens.trap: Starting here. That is the mockup drawn before the tokens.

full.cost: You inherit its visual choices, its weight and its upgrades. Getting out later costs more than getting in.
full.buys: Primitives that work with a keyboard and a screen reader from day one. That is the most underestimated work in this list.
full.wrong_when: When the brand is strong and specific: you will spend more time fighting the library than using it.

unstyled.option: Take an unstyled library, and dress it yourself
unstyled.cost: You write every appearance. The behaviour is given to you.
unstyled.buys: Accessibility and focus management without inheriting a visual identity. The best ratio for a brand of your own.
unstyled.wrong_when: On three screens: setting it up costs more than it protects.

own.cost: Accessibility is entirely yours. Focus traps, screen reader announcements, focus restoration: it is a craft.
own.buys: No dependency, no inheritance. Justified when the product IS its interface.
own.wrong_when: Almost always, at the start. It is the choice that looks cheapest and is not.

design_system.mockup_head: « Do we draw the mockup first? »
design_system.mockup_blurb: Short answer: a mockup, yes. THE finished mockup, no.
design_system.mockup_note:
An exploratory mockup is drawn right now — on paper, in grey, with no precise value. It exists to agree on what the product does, and that is exactly what phase 1 of a spec asks for.

A finished mockup drawn before the tokens invents a scale. Spacings picked by eye, half a dozen slightly different greys, three type sizes close together. The code copies them, because it has nothing else to refer to. You then do not have a design system: you have a transcribed mockup, and the first change request is paid for everywhere.

The order that holds: agreement on what the product does → tokens → primitives → finished mockup built from the primitives that exist → screens. The mockup then becomes an assembly of things that exist, not an image to reproduce.
design_system.library_head: Write the primitives, or take an existing component library
design_system.library_blurb: The pipeline installs nothing: it argues and stops. This choice is submitted like any dependency, with its licence, its upkeep and its security surface.
design_system.library_note: The criterion that decides is accessibility. A library that handles neither focus, nor the keyboard, nor screen reader announcements is not a component library: it is a set of styles, and the hard work is still entirely ahead of you. Check that before the colours, not after.
design_system.title: What is settled before the first screen
design_system.lede: Four layers, and an order. The order is the content of this page: you do not reverse it afterwards without going over everything again.
design_system.verbatim: The pipeline does not choose for you. It explains, then makes your choice enforceable: once declared it is read back by a gate instead of being recalled in review.
design_system.already: Already in place: {library}. The choice below then reads as « keep or leave », and leaving costs more than entering.
design_system.layers_blurb: Each knows only the ones above it. A layer that jumps over its neighbour is an interface's first debt.
design_system.declare_note:
Three values in pipeline.config.json, under design_system: tokens (the path of the single source of truth), primitives (own, or the name of the library retained) and decided_at.

Without them, apply-profile refuses to run on a project with screens. The reason is the same as for the architecture: a choice that lives only in a page binds nobody, the agent taking the first issue will settle it alone, and every one after inherits it without anyone having approved it.

architecture.title: How should this project's code be arranged?
architecture.verbatim:
An architecture is where the files go and who is allowed to call whom. Nothing more. The complicated names are ways of answering those two questions.

The pipeline does not choose for you: the right answer depends on your product. It explains, then makes your choice enforceable — once declared, a file calling what it should not fails a gate instead of being flagged in review.
architecture.brief_head: First: what is this project about?
architecture.brief_blurb: Eight questions, in plain language. Answer them before looking at any architecture — that is what turns a generic recommendation into reasoned advice.
architecture.brief_note: The question that really decides is B3. A system that never refuses anything for a reason coming from the real world has no domain: it has a schema. And B4 checks that the refusals quoted really are refusals — « this field is required » is not one.
architecture.says_head: What your project says about itself
architecture.no_rule_found: No business rule found: this product stores and returns.
architecture.advice_blurb: Grounded in the analysis above, not in a general preference. The detail of each option is still further down.
architecture.glance_blurb: {count} options relevant to this project type. The detail is further down if you hesitate between two rows.
architecture.col_when: When it is the right call
architecture.axis_blurb: Answer them before looking at the names. They are answered without knowing any architecture, and they eliminate most of the options.
architecture.detail_blurb: {kept} retained out of {total}. The others are not bad: they solve problems this project type does not have.
architecture.reads_as: reads as: « {outer} may use {inner}{more}, never the reverse »
architecture.boundary_head: What crosses between the front and the back
architecture.boundary_blurb: On a full-stack repository this question counts for more than the internal structure of either side: it is what decides what breaks when one side moves.
architecture.wrong_head: « What if I get it wrong? »
architecture.wrong_blurb: That is the right objection. At the start of a project you do not know everything yet, and the files still have to go somewhere.
architecture.wrong_note:
Do not pick the heaviest option out of caution. That is the most common mistake: you pay immediately for insurance you may never claim, and the cost is taken out of every file you write, for years.

What decides is an asymmetry. Starting simple keeps the options open: you harden one folder the day it earns it, without touching the others. Starting complicated closes them: nobody removes layers, they endure them. A bad simple choice is corrected piece by piece; a bad heavy one, you live with.

Here, changing your mind is measured. Your architecture is declared in the configuration and checked by a gate. The day you change the declaration, the gate prints you the exact list of files that no longer obey the new rule. A migration becomes a task list, not an exploration — and that is the difference with a project where the architecture lives only in people's heads.
architecture.next_note:
Your choice becomes one line in the configuration: the folders, and who is allowed to call whom. The profile translates it into an automatically checked rule.

Worth knowing before you choose: changing architecture later means moving files across the whole project. The cheapest moment to decide is now, before the first line of code.
architecture.remaining_head: What your description does not yet say
architecture.remaining_blurb: Only these. The rest is already in what you wrote, and an option that turns on one of them is left undecided until it is answered rather than judged on silence.
architecture.remaining_none: Your description answers every question the decision turns on. Nothing below is judged on an absence.
architecture.removed_head: Removed by your project type, not by your analysis
architecture.removed_blurb: These are not offered above because you declared a {type} project. Your analysis has an opinion about them all the same, and hiding it would hide that the type declaration is what removed them.
architecture.removed_note: If one of these fits what you described, the type is what to reconsider — not the option.
architecture.type_help: The type filters the catalogue, so it is a decision:
architecture.type_decides: What decides between a web interface and a full-stack repository is the data: a web interface reads data it does not own. If this project holds its own database, it is fullstack.

spec.lede: What this spec built, what surfaced along the way, and what it cost. Computed from the store, not written by anyone.
spec.verbatim: Every line below comes from a record: the ledger QA observed in the environment, the findings each issue declared with the destination it named, the transitions with their stamps. No agent writes this page, so no agent can flatter it.
spec.built_head: What was built, and what proves it
spec.built_blurb: One entry per criterion, with the evidence observed in the environment — not the claim that it was.
spec.found_blurb: Nothing is lost and nothing is scheduled by surprise: each finding went where its destination said, and only one of the four creates work.
spec.cost_blurb: Read from the transition journal, never estimated. A step is bounded by three stamps, so the agent's turnaround and the validation are counted apart.
spec.cost_unknown: {count} step(s) carry no stamp: they were written before the journal recorded them, and are counted nowhere rather than as zero.
spec.unproved_blurb: Declared by each handoff, gathered here. Two issues of one spec once closed with the same hole and nobody could see it was the same one — a hole named twice is a hole worth a spec of its own.

B1.question: In one sentence, what is the product for, and for whom?
B1.hint: No jargon. If the sentence needs a technical word, it is describing the solution, not the need.
B1.reveals: the domain, and whether the product has an identifiable user

B2.question: Name three things a user does with it.
B2.hint: Actions, not screens. « borrow a book », not « the loan page ».
B2.reveals: the real operations, and whether they are more than storage

B3.question: Are there situations where the system must REFUSE something? Which ones?
B3.hint: Not required fields or formats. Real refusals: « this book is already out », « this account has too little ».
B3.reveals: THE question that detects a domain. No refusal of that kind, no domain.

B4.question: Would a professional in the field understand those refusals without any talk of software?
B4.hint: A librarian, an accountant. If they nod, it is domain. If they cannot see why you are telling them, it is data entry.
B4.reveals: whether the refusals are business rules or validation in disguise

B5.question: Does the product talk to outside systems? Might you replace one some day?
B5.hint: Database, payment, email delivery, third-party service. And above all: which one will you REALLY replace.
B5.reveals: whether ports are justified, or would be insurance you never claim

B6.question: How many people or agents will work on it at the same time?
B6.hint: Count pipeline agents as people: they get in each other's way the same way.
B6.reveals: whether the layout should optimise for cohesion or for parallel work

B7.question: In your previous projects, what changed most often?
B7.hint: Screens, rules, integrations. Answer from experience, not from intention.
B7.reveals: what belongs at the centre, and what belongs at the edge

B8.question: What will the product NOT do?
B8.hint: What is not named is assumed built. That is true from the first conversation.
B8.reveals: the real scope, and often a business rule hidden inside an exclusion

judgement.teams_parallel: Several teams in parallel: one folder each, nobody collides.
judgement.people_parallel: Several people in parallel: one folder each, nobody collides.
judgement.cheap: Almost no cost, and nothing forces you out of it until a precise pain demands it.
judgement.rules_fit: {count} business rule(s) found: they fit inside their feature folder for as long as they are not shared.
judgement.layered_parallel: Every feature crosses all three folders: with several people, everyone edits the same places.
judgement.layered_solo: Readable by one person, and familiar.
judgement.hex_none: No integration declared replaceable: ports would be insurance you never claim.
judgement.hex_many: {count} integrations you expect to replace: that is exactly the problem hexagonal solves.
judgement.hex_one: A single replaceable integration: isolate that one, not everything else.
judgement.clean_none: No business rule found: the layers would fill with objects copying rows around.
judgement.clean_dense: {count} business rules: dense enough to justify isolating them from any technology.
judgement.clean_thin: {count} business rule(s): that is an invariant to protect, not a domain to isolate. Protect it in the right place rather than adding layers.
judgement.sliced: Prevents circular imports in a codebase where everything tends to import everything.
judgement.mvvm: Screen logic is testable without launching the interface.
judgement.mvi_churn: Screens change often: reproducible state pays for itself.
judgement.mvi_stable: With no complicated screen state, the machinery costs more than it protects.
judgement.undecided: Undecidable while {question} is unanswered: the option turns on it, and silence is not a no.

generated.option: The back end generates the types, the front end uses them
generated.cost: A generation step, and a gate that refuses a stale contract.
generated.buys: The front end stops compiling once the back end changes its contract. The break shows at compile time, not at the user.
generated.wrong_when: When the two sides ship separately: the front end must then tolerate an older version of the back end.

shared.option: A shared folder of types, written by hand
shared.cost: Almost nothing, but synchronisation rests on vigilance.
shared.buys: Simple and readable, with no tooling.
shared.wrong_when: As soon as the contract changes often: the shared folder becomes wrong with nothing to report it.

redeclared.option: No sharing, the front end redeclares what it consumes
redeclared.buys: Each side evolves and ships alone. The front end declares exactly what it needs.
redeclared.wrong_when: When a single team holds both sides: you duplicate without gaining the independence that would justify it.
